records.topic: The Machine the Entire Chip Industry Depends On
records.coreQuestion: Why does the most advanced chipmaking run through one company's tin-plasma light machine?
records.openingLine: Every advanced chip depends on one machine.
records.secondBeat: Only one company builds and sells it.
records.dependency: Leading-edge chips at 5 and 3 nanometre process nodes depend on EUV exposure steps.
records.mechanism: A laser hits falling tin droplets to make a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light; mirrors in vacuum carry it to a reflective photomask.
records.bottleneck: A single supplier builds the complete system, and its tin-plasma source and vacuum mirror optics have no drop-in substitute.
records.failureConsequence: Without new EUV tools or service, fabs could not add leading-edge capacity; installed tools keep running only as long as maintenance and spares allow.
records.resilience: Service contracts, spare modules and slower multi-exposure deep-UV patterning are the fallbacks while alternative sources are developed.
records.expectedConsequence: leading-edge capacity stalls first; mature-node chips are largely unaffected
visualScenes: laser pulse hitting a tin droplet
editorialTitles: Why Only One Company Builds This Chip Machine
The Tin Droplets Behind Every Advanced Chip

facts.claim: EUV lithography uses 13.5 nm extreme ultraviolet light from a laser-pulsed tin plasma.
As of 2025, ASML is the only company that produces and sells EUV systems for chip production, targeting 5 nm and 3 nm process nodes.
The light source ejects molten tin droplets about 25 μm across at about 70 m/s through a vacuum chamber.
EUV light is absorbed by glass and air, so the systems use mirrors in vacuum instead of lenses.
Earlier deep-UV lithography used 193 nm light from argon fluoride lasers.

narration.text: Every advanced chip depends on one machine.
Only one company builds and sells it.
It uses extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nanometres.
Glass and air absorb that light, so everything runs in vacuum, on mirrors.
The light comes from molten tin droplets, blasted by a laser.
If this supply stops, there is no second vendor to call.
That is why one machine can shape a whole industry.

records.topic: The Garden-Hose-Thin Cables That Carry the Internet Across Oceans
records.coreQuestion: How does intercontinental internet traffic depend on thin cables lying on the seabed?
records.openingLine: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.
records.secondBeat: Deep-sea sections are only about 25 millimetres across.
records.dependency: Intercontinental internet and voice traffic runs mostly through fibre cables on the seabed.
records.mechanism: Light pulses travel through fibre pairs inside armoured deep-sea cable about 25 mm across, with repeaters boosting the signal along the route.
records.bottleneck: A cut cable must be located at sea, lifted and spliced by a specialised cable ship before its capacity returns.
records.failureConsequence: A break shifts traffic onto other cables; where spare capacity is thin, latency rises and some links slow until the repair ship arrives.
records.resilience: Route diversity, spare capacity on parallel cables, protection zones near shore and standing repair-ship agreements limit the damage.
records.expectedConsequence: traffic reroutes first; slowdowns depend on how much spare capacity parallel cables hold
visualScenes: cross-section of a deep-sea fibre cable
cable lying on the ocean floor
editorialTitles: The Internet Lies on the Ocean Floor
Why a Cut Cable Needs a Ship to Fix It

facts.claim: Modern submarine cables are typically about 25 mm in diameter and weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre in deep-sea sections.
By 1872 all continents except Antarctica had been linked by submarine telecommunications cables.
In 1873 a whale damaged the Persian Gulf Cable between Karachi and Gwadar.
Cable ships are limited to about eight knots while laying cable so it settles properly on the sea floor.
Eleven breaks occurred on early cables by 1860 because of storms, tides, sand movement and wear on rocks.
The Great Eastern laid the first cable to reach India from Aden in 1870.

narration.text: Your internet depends on hidden seabed cables.
Deep-sea sections are only about 25 millimetres across.
They weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre on the seabed.
Continents were already wired this way by 1872.
When one breaks, a cable ship must find the fault and splice it at sea.
Until then, traffic reroutes onto other cables, if they have room.
So repair ships are part of the internet too.

records.topic: The Slow Ships That Keep the Fast Internet Running
records.coreQuestion: Why do the internet's fastest links depend on a small fleet of slow, specialised ships?
records.openingLine: When an ocean cable breaks, who fixes it?
records.secondBeat: A cable ship does, and it lays new ones too.
records.dependency: Every new or broken submarine cable depends on a cable ship to lay or repair it.
records.mechanism: A cable ship pays out cable at low speed along a carefully mapped route, and in repairs grapples the cable from the seabed and splices it on deck.
records.bottleneck: Cable ships are purpose-built, carry specialised handling gear and trained crews, and cannot be improvised from ordinary vessels.
records.failureConsequence: When repair ships are busy or far away, a damaged cable stays down longer and traffic runs on thinner backup routes.
records.resilience: Regional maintenance agreements keep repair ships on standby, and route diversity keeps traffic moving while a repair waits.
records.expectedConsequence: repair time depends on how quickly a ship can reach the fault
visualScenes: cable ship paying out cable at the stern
mapped cable route on a sea chart
grapnel lifting a cable from the seabed
splicing a fibre cable on deck
editorialTitles: The Ships That Fix the Internet
Why Cable Ships Crawl at Eight Knots

facts.claim: Cable ships are limited to a speed of eight knots while laying cable so it lies properly on the sea floor.
A cable's position must be carefully mapped as it is laid.
In 1866 the SS Great Eastern successfully laid two transatlantic cables.
Oersted, built in 1872 for the Great Northern Telegraph Company, was the first ship specifically designed for cable repair.
USNS Zeus can lay about 1,600 km of cable to a depth of 2,700 m.
Cable engines can feed 240 m of cable a minute.
Goliath was the first ship to lay an ocean cable, in 1850.

narration.text: When an ocean cable breaks, who fixes it?
A cable ship does, and it lays new ones too.
It crawls at about eight knots so the cable settles.
Every metre of the route is mapped as it goes down.
In 1866, the Great Eastern laid two transatlantic cables.
By 1872, the first ship built just for cable repair appeared.
So the fastest links on Earth depend on its slowest ships.

records.topic: The 13 Names at the Top of the Internet
records.coreQuestion: How can thirteen root server names hold up every web address without a single point of failure?
records.openingLine: Every website depends on 13 hidden names.
records.secondBeat: They sit at the very top of DNS.
records.dependency: Every domain lookup ultimately relies on the DNS root zone served by thirteen named root servers.
records.mechanism: Resolvers ask a root server which top-level-domain servers to query; anycast spreads each root name across many server instances.
records.bottleneck: The thirteen names are fixed by the original 512-byte DNS packet limit, so resilience has to come from copies behind each name.
records.failureConsequence: Losing several instances barely matters; losing reachability to the whole root would slowly break lookups as cached answers expire.
records.resilience: Anycast copies worldwide, independent operators and resolver caching keep the root available even under attack.
records.expectedConsequence: cached answers hide short outages; only a long, total loss would be felt
editorialTitles: Why the Internet Has Exactly 13 Root Servers
The Hidden Directory Behind Every Website

facts.claim: There are 13 logical root name servers, named a through m under root-servers.net.
The choice of 13 came from the original DNS maximum packet size of 512 bytes over UDP.
Using anycast, the actual number of root server instances was 1954 as of December 5, 2025.
A 2003 survey reported that only 2% of all queries to the root servers were legitimate.

narration.text: Every website depends on 13 hidden names.
They sit at the very top of DNS.
Why only 13? The original DNS packet limit was 512 bytes.
But behind those names run 1,954 server copies worldwide.
Anycast sends each query to a nearby copy.
A 2003 survey found only 2% of root queries were legitimate.
That redundancy is why losing one server changes almost nothing.

records.topic: The Atom That Defines Every Second
records.coreQuestion: How does a microwave transition inside caesium atoms keep networks, navigation and grids on the same time?
records.openingLine: Why every second depends on caesium.
records.secondBeat: It's defined by vibrations inside caesium atoms.
records.dependency: The SI second, and every clock traced to it, depends on the caesium-133 transition.
records.mechanism: A caesium clock locks a microwave oscillator to the 9,192,631,770-cycle hyperfine transition of caesium-133 atoms.
records.bottleneck: Primary caesium standards are few, specialised instruments whose time is shared and compared between national laboratories.
records.failureConsequence: Without traceable reference clocks, networks, positioning and grid synchronisation would slowly drift apart.
records.resilience: Many independent laboratory clocks, satellite time transfer and local holdover oscillators keep time consistent through single failures.
records.expectedConsequence: clocks drift slowly first; systems needing tight synchronisation notice before anyone else
visualScenes: microwave cavity of an atomic clock
definition of the second text card
editorialTitles: What Actually Defines One Second
The Caesium Clock Behind Everyday Time

facts.claim: The second is the duration of 9192631770 periods of the radiation of the caesium-133 hyperfine transition, as defined by the 13th General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1967.
The radiation has a frequency of exactly 9.19263177 GHz and a wavelength of about 3.26 cm, in the microwave range.
Before 1967 the SI units of time were defined using the tropical year, and before 1960 by the mean solar day.
In 1983 the metre was defined indirectly in terms of the caesium standard.
The nucleus of caesium-133 has a nuclear spin of 7/2.
The meter was first defined between 1889 and 1960 by the international prototype meter.

narration.text: Why every second depends on caesium.
It's defined by vibrations inside caesium atoms.
One second is 9,192,631,770 cycles of their microwave radiation.
That definition has been official since 1967.
Before that, time came from Earth's own motion.
Since 1983, even the metre has depended on it.
So losing these clocks means networks, navigation and grids lose shared time.

records.topic: The 193-Kilometre Shortcut Europe and Asia Can't Replace
records.coreQuestion: Why does one canal through the Egyptian desert decide how fast Europe–Asia trade moves?
records.openingLine: Why one stuck ship stops Suez trade.
records.secondBeat: It's 193 kilometres of water through the Egyptian desert.
records.dependency: Europe–Asia shipping depends on the Suez Canal to avoid sailing around Africa.
records.mechanism: Ships transit in scheduled convoys through a single channel with limited passing sections, so one stuck vessel can stop traffic.
records.bottleneck: There is no parallel route of similar length; the alternative is the long voyage around the Cape of Good Hope.
records.failureConsequence: A closure strands ships at both ends, then forces rerouting that adds days to each voyage and disrupts schedules for weeks.
records.resilience: Widened passing sections, a second channel, salvage capacity and the Cape route as a slow fallback reduce the impact.
records.expectedConsequence: queues form within hours; schedule disruption lasts far longer than the blockage
visualScenes: satellite view of the Suez Canal
convoy of container ships in the canal
Cape of Good Hope detour map
queue of ships at the entrance
editorialTitles: Why One Stuck Ship Can Stop World Trade
The Canal Europe and Asia Can't Replace

facts.claim: The Suez Canal is 193.3 kilometres long and is a key trade route between Europe and Asia.
An expansion was intended to nearly double the canal's capacity from 49 to 97 ships per day.
In 2004 the canal was closed for three days when the oil tanker Tropic Brilliance became stuck.
Following the grounding of the Ever Given in 2021, Egypt accelerated plans to extend and widen the canal's second channel.
After the Six-Day War, an Egyptian blockade kept the canal closed for eight years.
In 2021 more than 20,600 vessels traversed the canal, an average of 56 per day.
Construction lasted from 1859 to 1869, and the canal opened on 17 November 1869.
The Suez Canal Authority opened a new side channel in 2016.

narration.text: Why one stuck ship stops Suez trade.
It's 193 kilometres of water through the Egyptian desert.
Its expansion aimed to lift capacity to 97 ships a day.
In 2004, one stuck tanker closed it for three days.
In 2021, the grounded Ever Given pushed Egypt to widen it again.
After the Six-Day War, it stayed closed for eight years.
Every alternative means sailing around Africa.

records.topic: The Canal That Runs on Lake Water
records.coreQuestion: Why does every ship crossing Panama depend on how much fresh water is in the lakes above the locks?
records.openingLine: Every Panama crossing depends on lake water.
records.secondBeat: The locks lift ships 26 metres, using gravity alone.
records.dependency: Every Panama Canal transit depends on fresh water from the lakes above the locks.
records.mechanism: Culverts in the lock walls let lake water flow by gravity into each chamber to raise ships, then drain it toward the sea to lower them.
records.bottleneck: Each lockage spends a chamber of lake water, so the number of transits is limited by how full the lakes are.
records.failureConsequence: In a dry season, water limits reduce daily transits and draft allowances, forcing ships to wait, lighten loads or reroute.
records.resilience: Water-saving basins, draft limits, reservoir management and transit slot rationing stretch the water that is available.
records.expectedConsequence: a dry year cuts crossings first; costs rise as ships queue or divert
visualScenes: Gatun Lake and lock layout map
editorialTitles: Why the Panama Canal Needs Rain
The Lake Water Behind Every Panama Crossing

facts.claim: The Panama Canal locks lift ships up 85 feet (26 metres) to the main elevation of the canal and lower them again.
Each lock chamber requires 26,700,000 US gallons (101,000 m3) of water to fill.
The water is moved by gravity through culverts from the lake into the chambers, and from each chamber down to the next or to the sea.
The first trial lockage of the Gatun Locks was made on September 26, 1913.

narration.text: Every Panama crossing depends on lake water.
The locks lift ships 26 metres, using gravity alone.
Filling one chamber takes about 101,000 cubic metres of water.
That water flows down from the lake above, through giant culverts.
Each lowering then sends it on toward the sea.
The locks first lifted a test vessel in 1913.
So a dry year means fewer ships can cross.

records.topic: The Chemical Reaction That Feeds Billions
records.coreQuestion: How does one high-pressure reaction turn air and natural gas into the fertilizer behind modern harvests?
records.openingLine: Why your food depends on natural gas.
records.secondBeat: This reaction pulls nitrogen from air to make fertilizer.
records.dependency: Most nitrogen fertilizer, and the crop yields built on it, depends on ammonia from the Haber process.
records.mechanism: Nitrogen from air reacts with hydrogen over an iron catalyst at about 200 bar and 500 °C to form ammonia.
records.bottleneck: The plants are large, high-pressure installations that need cheap hydrogen, usually from natural gas.
records.failureConsequence: When natural gas becomes scarce or expensive, ammonia output falls, fertilizer prices rise and farmers apply less the next season.
records.resilience: Fertilizer stocks, diversified gas supply, imported ammonia and more efficient fertilizer use buffer short disruptions.
records.expectedConsequence: fertilizer prices react first; yields follow a season later
visualScenes: gas price to food price chain
editorialTitles: How Air Becomes Fertilizer
Why Natural Gas Is Part of Your Food

facts.claim: The Haber process converts atmospheric nitrogen to ammonia by reaction with hydrogen using an iron catalyst.
Atmospheric nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air but is exceptionally stable.
Most plants continue to use the original process conditions of about 200 bar and 500 °C.
Ammonia production accounts for 1–2% of global energy consumption and 3% to 5% of natural gas consumption.
The process enabled the global population to increase from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by November 2018.
A single pass through the reactor yields only about 15% ammonia.
Recycling leftover reactants eventually achieves 97% conversion.

narration.text: Why your food depends on natural gas.
This reaction pulls nitrogen from air to make fertilizer.
Air is 78% nitrogen, but that nitrogen barely reacts.
So plants force it at about 200 bar and 500 degrees.
It uses 3 to 5% of the world's natural gas.
Its fertilizer helped population grow from 1.6 to 7.7 billion.
That's why a gas shortage turns into a food problem.

records.topic: The Network That Carries the World's Payment Messages
records.coreQuestion: How can a network that never holds money still be able to cut an economy off from global payments?
records.openingLine: Why banks depend on one hidden network.
records.secondBeat: It never holds the money, only the payment messages.
records.dependency: Cross-border bank payments depend on standardised SWIFT messages between institutions.
records.mechanism: Banks exchange standardised payment instructions over SWIFT; settlement itself happens through accounts held elsewhere.
records.bottleneck: Replacing it means every counterparty adopting another messaging system, identifier scheme and security setup at once.
records.failureConsequence: A bank cut off from the network can still hold money but struggles to instruct payments abroad, isolating its customers.
records.resilience: Alternative domestic messaging systems, correspondent workarounds and contingency channels exist but cover only part of the traffic.
records.expectedConsequence: cross-border payments slow or stop first; domestic payments largely continue
visualScenes: payment message flow between two banks
difference between message and settlement diagram
editorialTitles: The Network Behind Almost Every International Payment
Why SWIFT Never Touches Your Money

facts.claim: In 2015 SWIFT linked more than 11,000 financial institutions in over 200 countries and territories.
Its members were exchanging an average of over 32 million messages per day.
As of 2018, around half of all high-value cross-border payments worldwide used the SWIFT network.
SWIFT is a cooperative established in 1973 in Belgium and owned by its member banks and firms.
SWIFT does not manage accounts for individuals or institutions and does not hold funds from third parties.
SWIFT was founded in Brussels on 3 May 1973.
It was initially supported by 239 banks in 15 countries.
After a payment is initiated, it must be settled through a payment system such as T2 in Europe.
SWIFT assigns ISO 9362 Business Identifier Codes, popularly known as SWIFT codes.

narration.text: Why banks depend on one hidden network.
It never holds the money, only the payment messages.
In 2015, it linked over 11,000 institutions in more than 200 countries.
Together they sent over 32 million messages a day.
By 2018, about half of high-value cross-border payments used it.
It began in 1973 as a Belgian cooperative owned by banks.
That's why being cut off from it can isolate a whole economy.

records.topic: The Six-Hour Isotope Behind Millions of Scans
records.coreQuestion: Why do tens of millions of medical scans depend on a few research reactors and a tracer that decays within hours?
records.openingLine: Why hospitals can't stockpile this isotope.
records.secondBeat: Technetium-99m fades by half every six hours.
records.dependency: Tens of millions of diagnostic scans a year depend on technetium-99m made from reactor-produced molybdenum-99.
records.mechanism: Molybdenum-99 from uranium fission in research reactors decays into technetium-99m, which hospitals extract from generators and inject as a tracer.
records.bottleneck: Molybdenum-99 is made in a small number of research reactors, and neither it nor the tracer can be stockpiled.
records.failureConsequence: When a producing reactor goes offline, supply drops within days and hospitals postpone or ration scans.
records.resilience: Coordinated reactor maintenance schedules, additional producers and alternative production routes reduce shortages.
records.expectedConsequence: scan capacity drops within days; nothing can be pulled from storage
editorialTitles: The Medical Isotope You Can't Stockpile
Why a Reactor Outage Cancels Scans Abroad

facts.claim: Technetium-99m is used in tens of millions of medical diagnostic procedures annually, the most commonly used medical radioisotope.
Its half-life is 6.0066 hours, meaning 93.7% of it decays within 24 hours.
It is produced from molybdenum-99, which has a longer half-life of 2.75 days.
Molybdenum-99 is usually created by fission of highly enriched uranium in a small number of research and materials testing reactors in several countries.

narration.text: Why hospitals can't stockpile this isotope.
Technetium-99m fades by half every six hours.
It's used in tens of millions of scans every year.
Within a day, 93.7% of it has decayed.
It comes from molybdenum-99, which lasts only days.
That parent is made in a small number of research reactors.
That's why one reactor outage can cancel scans far away.

records.topic: The 39-Kilometre Gap a Quarter of Seaborne Oil Must Pass
records.coreQuestion: Why does a strait about 39 kilometres wide carry so much of the world's oil and gas?
records.openingLine: 25% of seaborne oil depends on one strait.
records.secondBeat: It's the Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman.
records.dependency: A quarter of seaborne oil trade and a fifth of the world's LNG depend on passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
records.mechanism: Tankers follow a traffic separation scheme of two lanes, each about 3.7 kilometres wide, through a strait bordered by Iran and Oman.
records.bottleneck: Gulf exporters have few pipeline routes that bypass the strait, so most of their tanker traffic has no alternative.
records.failureConsequence: Any threat to passage raises insurance and freight costs immediately; a real closure would remove supply faster than reserves could replace it.
records.resilience: Bypass pipelines, strategic petroleum reserves, naval escorts and other producers cover part of a disruption.
records.expectedConsequence: prices react to the threat before any supply is lost
visualScenes: satellite map of the Strait of Hormuz
tanker lanes of the traffic separation scheme
share of oil and LNG graphic
editorialTitles: Why a Quarter of Seaborne Oil Passes One Strait
The Narrow Gap That Moves Oil Prices

facts.claim: The Strait of Hormuz is about 167 km long, with a width varying from about 97 km to 39 km.
During 2023–2025, 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas and 25% of seaborne oil trade passed through the strait annually.
Ships follow a traffic separation scheme in which each lane is 2 nautical miles (3.7 km) wide.
Iran in 1959 and Oman in 1972 expanded their territorial seas to 12 nautical miles.

narration.text: 25% of seaborne oil depends on one strait.
It's the Strait of Hormuz, between Iran and Oman.
It also carries 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas.
At its narrowest, the strait is about 39 kilometres wide.
Tankers use two lanes, each just 3.7 kilometres wide.
Both countries claim 12 nautical miles of sea there.
That's why any threat here moves oil prices worldwide.

records.topic: The 2,000-Tonne Cranes Every Container Passes Under
records.coreQuestion: Why can't a port simply add or replace the giant cranes that unload every container ship?
records.openingLine: Every container depends on this crane.
records.secondBeat: Ship-to-shore cranes lift every box off the ship.
records.dependency: Container ports depend on ship-to-shore cranes to move every box between ship and quay.
records.mechanism: A gantry crane runs on quay rails and lifts containers with a telescopic spreader, up to two 20-foot boxes at a time.
records.bottleneck: The cranes are enormous, custom-built machines sized to the port's rails and ships, so replacements take long to build and ship.
records.failureConsequence: Losing cranes at a busy terminal slows every vessel at the berth, and queues spread to the next ports on the route.
records.resilience: Spare cranes at other berths, maintenance programmes and moving ships to other terminals absorb single failures.
records.expectedConsequence: berth productivity drops first; ship queues follow
visualScenes: ship-to-shore crane over a container ship
editorialTitles: The Giant Cranes Behind Everything You Buy
Why Ports Can't Buy a Spare Crane Overnight

facts.claim: A modern container crane capable of lifting two 20-foot containers at once generally has a rated lifting capacity of 65 tonnes.
Post-Panamax cranes weigh approximately 800–900 tonnes, while super-post-Panamax cranes can weigh 1,600–2,000 tonnes.
Gantry rail gauges were typically 12 to 16 meters; as ships grew they increased to 33 m.
As ships grew in size, more cranes were assigned to each ship and docks had to get wider.

narration.text: Every container depends on this crane.
Ship-to-shore cranes lift every box off the ship.
One can lift two 20-foot containers at once.
Its rated load is about 65 tonnes.
The newest giants weigh up to 2,000 tonnes each.
Their rails grew from 16 to 33 metres apart as ships grew.
That's why a port can't just buy a spare overnight.
